issues.legal_issue: A waqf-alal-aulad created under Shia law is a valid waqf where its terms dedicate the property for recognized religious, pious, or charitable purposes, even if most income benefits the waqif’s descendants.
A waqf-alal-aulad was compulsorily registrable under the applicable waqf legislation even if it was otherwise excluded from that legislation’s substantive provisions.
A compromise of proceedings relating to waqf property without the Waqf Board’s required sanction is invalid.
A transfer of waqf property made without the Waqf Board’s prior sanction, contrary to a statutory prohibition, is void.
Article 96 of the Limitation Act applies to a valuable-consideration transfer by a waqf manager only if the transfer is not void, and does not govern a void transfer.
A beneficiary of a waqf is not barred from acquiring title to waqf property by adverse possession merely because of beneficiary status.
Article 65 of the Limitation Act applies to possession following a void transfer, with limitation running from the date of the transfer.
Section 107 of the Waqf Act does not revive title to waqf property that was extinguished by adverse possession before that provision came into force.
A proceeding under Section 52 of the Waqf Act cannot displace title already acquired through adverse possession under the applicable limitation law.
